audit.evidenceText: The Pudding Cup Skip to main content The Pudding Cup The best visual and data-driven stories of 2026 To be completely honest: we almost didn’t do it this year. Over the last year, we’ve felt the same AI fatigue a lot of you probably have. Our inboxes and feeds have been flooded. The Pudding has always been about more than just a shiny end result. It’s about what it took to get there: the ambition, the struggle, the triumph, and the hope of sharing a discovery. We’re not here to police how you create a visual data-driven story, but if your project doesn’t have a heartbeat, it’s not getting the Cup! So, the submissions are open… for now. But if we find ourselves drowning in slop, we’ll close the form, and figure out how to reinvent the Cup into something entirely different that maintains our values. We really hope we don't have to. Here’s what you need to know: Entries are free , just give us a URL! (One per person, please) Must be your own work Must have been published / put on the internet in 2026 Highly encouraged to share your process and raw materials Up to three winners will each receive $1,500 . Deadline - Monday, November 30, 2026 Winners Announced - The week of December 07, 2026 More info in the form, but hit us up at sup@pudding.cool with questions! candidates.title: ArcPy

audit.pageDescription: ArcPy is a Python site package for performing geographic information system (GIS) functions available in ArcGIS.
audit.evidenceText: What is ArcPy?—ArcGIS Pro | Documentation Back to Top ArcPy is a Python site package that provides a useful and productive way to perform geographic data analysis, data conversion, data management, and map automation with Python. This package provides a rich and native Python experience offering code completion (type a keyword and a dot to get a pop-up list of properties and methods supported by that keyword; select one to insert it) and reference documentation for each function, module, and class. The additional power of using ArcPy is that Python is a general-purpose programming language. It is interpreted and dynamically typed and is suited for interactive work and quick prototyping of one-off programs known as scripts while being powerful enough to write large applications in. ArcGIS applications written with ArcPy benefit from the development of additional modules in numerous niches of Python by GIS professionals and programmers from many different disciplines. audit.pageDescription: Ahead of Election Day, the tool has ingested 25 million TikTok videos and 500,000 podcasts to gain new insight into U.S. voters.
audit.evidenceText: The Wall Street Journal’s new AI tool, “Doppler,” forecasts the issues that will shape the midterm elections | Nieman Journalism Lab Get Nieman Lab in your inbox. All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Subscribe another address The Wall Street Journal’s new AI tool, “Doppler,” forecasts the issues that will shape the midterm elections Ahead of Election Day, the tool has ingested 25 million TikTok videos and 500,000 podcasts to gain new insight into U.S. voters. (Courtesy of The Wall Street Journal) By Andrew Deck Oct. 21, 2026, 3:05 p.m. More than 100 million voters are expected to cast ballots in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. In recent election cycles, political reporting based on voter polling has drawn criticism , prompted scrutiny , and found defenders . As the debate over the value of polling continues, The Wall Street Journal is exploring new ways to cover public opinion and break out of traditional horse race political coverage . In late September, the Journal published its first story using Doppler News AI, a custom tool built to help expand the publication’s midterms coverage. So far, Doppler has ingested more than 25 million TikTok videos, roughly 500,000 podcast episodes, and thousands of Instagram videos and cable news segments. The Journal uses the tool to monitor trends across the internet and to identify voter priorities, concerns, and sentiments that traditional polling might miss. RELATED ARTICLE How The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere” Andrew Deck February 11, 2026 “We’re not trying to predict the election, but people encounter politics through a lot of different lanes: culture, work, money, family, community. We wanted to tap into that and listen in on those conversations,” said Aja Whitaker-Moore , the deputy editor-in-chief of the Journal. “We’re taking a massive set of information…and telling you, from a statistical standpoint: ‘Here’s what people are talking about. Here are the questions they’re asking. Here are the places where those conversations are happening.'” Other newsrooms have leaned on AI “ visibility tools ” in the past to support their reporting. That includes using large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and summarize “manosphere” podcasts , school board meetings , and local talk radio shows . But Doppler goes further. Rather than using AI-generated summaries to generate leads or help beat reporters monitor online content more efficiently, the Journal uses Doppler to conduct large-scale AI analyses quickly — and publishes those insights for readers. So far, analyses produced by Doppler have led to four major midterms stories in the Journal, with more expected to run before Election Day. For now, each story requires a custom treatment, with engineers and data journalists working alongside the D.C. politics team to refine the methodology, toggle on and off different features, and audit the results. “The tool is only as good as the questions that you ask it,” said Whitaker-Moore. The Journal holds a weekly editorial meeting leading up to Election Day to workshop story angles and find new threads to explore. @wallstreetjournal A new in-house AI tool lets WSJ reporters analyze trends in online conversation to help understand the political mood of the country ahead of the midterm elections. A previous post paired a visual of TikToks from across the internet with a headline that identified them as conservative podcasters. ♬ original sound – The Wall Street Journal A story published on October 8 analyzed over 30,000 hours of podcasts and documented how, in recent weeks, right-leaning podcasters had started discussing “affordability” as often as left-leaning podcasters, despite President Trump calling the affordability crisis a “hoax.” Another story published on October 1 traced anti-AI sentiment, including opposition to Flock surveillance cameras , by analyzing more than four million TikTok videos and thousands of hours of podcasts. The Journal found that posters who shared anti-Flock sentiments disagreed on other political positions about 12% of the time, three times the average rate across other political topics tracked — putting the issue “at the top of the list of positions that unite creators who are otherwise at odds.” For a story published on October 15 , the Journal pulled content about 67 Democratic politicians from its Doppler database. The analysis showed that the Democratic politician currently receiving the most favorable commentary is Angie Nixon, the progressive Senate nominee in Florida. About 70% of TikTok videos posted about her in recent weeks were favorable. She was followed by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff at 54%. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ranked the lowest in the analysis; just 3% of videos posted about him were favorable. Courtesy of The Wall Street Journal Whitaker-Moore said the idea for Doppler was inspired by conversations with Washington bureau chief Damian Paletta and politics editor Christopher Matthews . They thought the coverage of the 2024 U.S. election missed important undercurrents in public opinion that never surfaced in polling. And though reporters acknowledged the power of podcasts in that election cycle, there weren’t many standardized ways to capture what was being said across those channels. Coming out of those conversations, Whitaker-Moore posed a question to Rob Barry , who leads the Journal’s data journalism team: “Can you build something that can eat the internet and then feed it back to us?” The Journal had already built its own podcast transcription and summarization tool, Orca. (The name refers to the tight-knit pods in which orcas travel.) Orca had collected countless hours of audio and YouTube videos, not just of political podcasts but from genres like health and wellness. RELATED ARTICLE What can The Wall Street Journal’s new ad campaign tell us about its future? Sarah Scire June 11, 2024 The Journal’s experience with TikTok-based investigations made the social media platform’s videos another natural source of information for Doppler. It’s nearly impossible to create a comprehensive database of TikTok videos, or even a truly random sample. Instead, Barry’s team used a monitoring tool that relies on TikTok’s own recommendation algorithms to identify the accounts it should track. “Every day we’re adding tons of data across all the different platforms that we’re looking at,” Barry told me. “The database is growing in the background constantly.” To make sense of that data, Doppler has a tech stack that includes different types of AI models, including LLMs. The model used depends on the specific reporting question. Embedding models have been central to some of stories published so far. These AI models convert text or images into vectors — lists of numbers that capture the meaning of each piece of content. By vectorizing the content, Doppler can map out the ideas in a dataset and see where they naturally cluster together. The Journal’s data journalism team has used vectorization in the past, including in its Pulitzer Prize–winning story that mapped out Elon Musk’s entire history of tweets . In Doppler, vectorization facilitates a kind of internet radar, helping reporters identify where patterns are forming across its social media and podcasting database. For now, the Journal’s political reporters can’t just start using Doppler on their own. The exact methodology has been tailored to each story published, with the help of engineers. RELATED ARTICLE Local newsrooms are using AI to listen in on public meetings Andrew Deck March 13, 2025 “There’s a lot of human judgment in this. My team would not have aimed for a tool that seeks to just produce stuff that we then put directly on the internet,” Barry said. “You still need that human intermediary, that human to apply the judgment and to ask the question.” The Journal is attaching a short methodology to every story assisted by Doppler. It makes clear that AI was used to produce the piece, briefly explains how the analysis came together, and notes some of the tool’s limitations. Despite manual spot checks of data classifications and other safeguards to make sure the tool’s outputs are accurate, Barry said, “there’s almost always going to be some level of error and uncertainty and blur around the edges.” The disclosures are one way to “give readers a sense for what that level of issue is.” Looking ahead, the Journal is considering bringing Doppler to other desks in the newsroom. The data being collected is not inherently political, and it could be used to help answer a host of other reporting questions, drawing on insights scattered across the internet. “We definitely think that [Doppler News AI] can live beyond the midterms and live beyond elections,” Whitaker-Moore said. candidates.title: Cloud-Native Geospatial, COG

audit.evidenceText: Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF A Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) is a regular GeoTIFF file, aimed at being hosted on a HTTP file server, with an internal organization that enables more efficient workflows on the cloud. It does this by leveraging the ability of clients issuing ​ HTTP GET range requests to ask for just the parts of a file they need. Learn More Efficient Imagery Data Access COG-aware software can stream just the portion of data that it needs, improving processing times and creating real-time workflows previously not possible Reduced Duplication of Data Accessing COGs with cloud workflows enables diverse software to all access a single file online instead of needing to copy and cache the data Legacy Compatibility Traditional GIS software is able to treat Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs just like normal GeoTIFFs, so data providers need only produce one format Tools QGIS 3.2 has stellar COG support, with an option to select online files in the data import, including authentication for private data (tutorial coming soon). Older versions can read Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs using Virtual Raster Builder with a vsicurl file format to refer to the online URL. See the tutorial for details. COG-Explorer is a browser app to visualize Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, for example from the Landsat-8 archive on S3, based on geotiff.js . Marblecutter serves web tiles from Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, completely on the fly. You can see it in action at OpenAerialMap , as all tiles are rendered by an early version. tiles.rdnt.io is an instance of Marblecutter running on lambda , hosted by Radiant.Earth, that anyone can use. It powers the map at cogeo.org/map . Rio-cogeo is a Rasterio plugin to create and validate Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. Rio-tiler is a Rasterio plugin to read mercator tiles from Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. Used to create serverless tile servers with lambda-tiler . TiTiler is a lightweight service for creating map tiles from Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. It's a set of Python modules that lets you build your own dynamic tile services using FastAPI. maplibre-cog-protocol is a plugin for MapLibre GL JS that enables displaying Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs on an interactive MapLibre map without an intermediate server. Rio-glui Rasterio plugin that helps explore Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF in your web browser. Google Earth Engine now supports output of COGs from any Earth Engine operation, see: Exporting - Configuration Parameters . Earth Engine supports reading COG data hosted on Google Cloud Storage, see: COG-backed Earth Engine Assets . GRASS GIS can read Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs by using Virtual Raster Builder with a vsicurl file format to refer to the online URL and registration within GRASS GIS using r.external . Radiant.Earth is hosting a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF validator . You can also get the source code , created by Even Rouault with support from Planet . COGDumper is an open source python library to read COG's internal tiles. It's a lightweight library that doesn't need GDAL, and can be installed with pip install cogdumper . Maxar delivers tiled COGs of their satellite imagery through their Analysis Ready Data (ARD) product line. See their blog post for more information. Monteverdi , the Orfeo ToolBox image viewer, can navigate in remote Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF out of the box. GeoServer can leverage COGs by using the COG Support community module. RasterFrames brings the power of Spark DataFrames to geospatial raster data, and is able to read Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs using GeoTrellis . Farmshots builds agriculture analytics on top of Planet’s Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, pulling in just the needed field data and serving it up live to their customers. Earth Observing System ’s Engine and Land Viewer are both able to leverage Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs for live web tile serving and on the fly band math. Geopera ’s Imagery Portal utilizes Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs for quick access to specific subsets of large datasets, reducing bandwith and allowing faster rendering and processing times. Terracotta is a flexible, open-source tile server that you can use to view and serve your Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs as web layers. Supports serverless architectures and serving COGs from S3 buckets. Terrabit 's Albatross Platform utilizes Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs to display compressed, browser-accessible previews of analysis-ready geospatial datasets, enabling teams to visually inspect and validate data quality before committing to large data transfers. WebODM is a user-friendly, extendable application and API for processing aerial imagery capable of serving Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. ODM is a command line toolkit to process aerial imagery and is capable of generating Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs as 2D outputs. GeoTiffCOG C# is a C# Library for querying GeoTIFF files, including Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. Cogger is a command line utility and library that produces a COG from a tiled GeoTIFF. It works by shuffling the original GeoTIFF file's bytes, and is therefore very fast as it does not induce an imagery recompression. Cogger is written in go, cross-platform, and does not depend on GDAL. NextGIS is a full SaaS stack of geospatial software: desktop, web and mobile. NextGIS Web (server) is able to create and serve Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. NextGIS Connect (QGIS plugin) is able to upload to NextGIS Web and add COGs back to QGIS in one click (with the style if any). Details cog-validator-java is a Java-based tool for validating COGs. It ensures COGs meet required specifications and provides detailed error messages for correction. Ideal for Java developers. Libraries GDAL was the project that started Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, by leveraging the vsicurl driver , so both reading and writing COGs is well supported. See the GDAL Wiki for how to read COGs with GDAL. geotiff.js is a small library to parse TIFF files for visualization or analysis, including Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. It is written in pure JavaScript, and is usable in both the browser and node.js applications. Rasterio wraps the powerful features of GDAL in idiomatic Python functions and classes. Their latest release includes a number of features to optimize Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF access. See their Advanced Rasterio Features Notebook for truly excellent documentation on working with COGs. GeoTrellis is a scalable Scala geospatial library, that can create and read Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. Head over to the documentation. And check out Eugene Cheipesh's FOSS4G-NA 2018 talk on COGs. GeoTools is the leading Java geospatial library, and it supports COGs with the s3-geotiff module. Apache Spatial Information System (SIS) is a Java geospatial library capable of reading COGs over HTTP or S3. COG images can be part of a chain of operations such as raster reprojection, which will read only the tiles requested by the final output. Orfeo ToolBox All Orfeo ToolBox applications can read Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs through GDAL (simply prefix the file url with /vsicurl/) Most any software that relies on GDAL should support Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs without much effort. Things like MapServer, Safe FME, ArcGIS and ENVI jump to mind. The fact that they and others aren't on this list mostly means no one has tested and got them working yet. Feel free to submit a pull request to add any software confirmed to support COGs (links to documentation appreciated!). OpenAerialMap stores all new imagery as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, and also provides a service that takes uploaded data and turns it in to AWS S3 hosted COGs. The only constraint is that data uploaded must be openly licensed. Planet provides all its data (from RapidEye, PlanetScope and soon SkySat satellites) as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs. DigitalGlobe ’s GBDX data is available as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, for all processing done on the platform. And their blog post explains how IKONOS and NOAA’s VIIRS night lights data are available as COG CBERS on AWS has converted all CBERS-4 data to Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. SpaceNet data is all available as COG. You can browse the data on their STAC Browser instance . ISERV data from NASA has been made available by Radiant.Earth as a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. You can browse the data on their STAC Browser instance . Mundi offers a wide range of EO data as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. A collection of Copernicus Sentinel-1 GRD files is available as COG, and Mundi provides other collections on demand. As a part of the OGC standard, adoption of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs increases over time, allowing more software and tools to support the standard natively. Here is the standard: OGC COG Specification . For more details, visit the OGC GitHub Profile .

audit.pageTitle: Beautiful Soup: We called him Tortoise because he taught us.
audit.pageDescription: Beautiful Soup: a library designed for screen-scraping HTML and XML.
audit.evidenceText: Beautiful Soup: We called him Tortoise because he taught us. [ Download | Documentation | Hall of Fame | For enterprise | Source | Changelog | Discussion group | Zine ] Beautiful Soup You didn't write that awful page. You're just trying to get some data out of it. Beautiful Soup is here to help. Since 2004, it's been saving programmers hours or days of work on quick-turnaround screen scraping projects. Beautiful Soup is a Python library designed for quick turnaround projects like screen-scraping. Three features make it powerful: Beautiful Soup provides a few simple methods and Pythonic idioms for navigating, searching, and modifying a parse tree: a toolkit for dissecting a document and extracting what you need. It doesn't take much code to write an application Beautiful Soup automatically converts incoming documents to Unicode and outgoing documents to UTF-8. You don't have to think about encodings, unless the document doesn't specify an encoding and Beautiful Soup can't detect one. Then you just have to specify the original encoding. Beautiful Soup sits on top of popular Python parsers like lxml and html5lib , allowing you to try out different parsing strategies or trade speed for flexibility. Beautiful Soup parses anything you give it, and does the tree traversal stuff for you. You can tell it "Find all the links", or "Find all the links of class externalLink ", or "Find all the links whose urls match "foo.com", or "Find the table heading that's got bold text, then give me that text." Valuable data that was once locked up in poorly-designed websites is now within your reach. Projects that would have taken hours take only minutes with Beautiful Soup. Interested? Read more. Getting and giving support Beautiful Soup for enterprise available via Tidelift If you have questions, send them to the discussion group . If you find a bug, file it on Launchpad . If it's a security vulnerability, report it confidentially through Tidelift . If you use Beautiful Soup as part of your work, please consider a Tidelift subscription . This will support many of the free software projects your organization depends on, not just Beautiful Soup. If Beautiful Soup is useful to you on a personal level, you might like to read Tool Safety , a short zine I wrote about what I learned about software development from working on Beautiful Soup. Thanks! Download Beautiful Soup The current release is Beautiful Soup 4.14.3 (November 30, 2025). You can install Beautiful Soup 4 with pip install beautifulsoup4 . In Debian and Ubuntu, Beautiful Soup is available as the python3-bs4 package. In Fedora it's available as the python3-beautifulsoup4 package. Beautiful Soup is licensed under the MIT license, so you can also download the tarball, drop the bs4/ directory into almost any Python application (or into your library path) and start using it immediately. Beautiful Soup 4 is supported on Python versions 3.7 and greater. Support for Python 2 was discontinued on January 1, 2021—one year after the Python 2 sunsetting date. Beautiful Soup 3 Beautiful Soup 3 was the official release line of Beautiful Soup from May 2006 to March 2012. It does not support Python 3 and was discontinued or January 1, 2021—one year after the Python 2 sunsetting date. If you have any active projects using Beautiful Soup 3, you should migrate to Beautiful Soup 4 as part of your Python 3 conversion. Soon, the beautifulsoup PyPI package name will be reclaimed by a more recent version of Beautiful Soup. When that happens, all Python 2 code still using Beautiful Soup 3 will break. Here's the Beautiful Soup 3 documentation. The current and hopefully final release of Beautiful Soup 3 is 3.2.2 (October 5, 2019). It's the BeautifulSoup package on pip. It's also available as python-beautifulsoup in Debian and Ubuntu, and as python-BeautifulSoup in Fedora. Beautiful Soup 3, like Beautiful Soup 4, is supported through Tidelift . Hall of Fame Over the years, Beautiful Soup has been used in hundreds of different projects. There's no way I can list them all, but I want to highlight a few high-profile projects. Beautiful Soup isn't what makes these projects interesting, but it did make their completion easier: "Movable Type" , a work of digital art on display in the lobby of the New York Times building, uses Beautiful Soup to scrape news feeds. Jiabao Lin's DXY-COVID-19-Crawler uses Beautiful Soup to scrape a Chinese medical site for information about COVID-19, making it easier for researchers to track the spread of the virus. (Source: "How open source software is fighting COVID-19" ) Reddit uses Beautiful Soup to parse a page that's been linked to and find a representative image . Alexander Harrowell uses Beautiful Soup to track the business activities of an arms merchant. The developers of Python itself used Beautiful Soup to migrate the Python bug tracker from Sourceforge to Roundup . The Lawrence Journal-World uses Beautiful Soup to gather statewide election results . The NOAA's Forecast Applications Branch uses Beautiful Soup in TopoGrabber , a script for downloading "high resolution USGS datasets." If you've used Beautiful Soup in a project you'd like me to know about, please do send email to me or the discussion group . Development Development happens at Launchpad . You can get the source code or file bugs . This document is part of Crummy, the webspace of Leonard Richardson ( contact information ). Assertions automatically retry until conditions are met. No artificial timeouts, no flaky tests. Test isolation Each test gets a fresh browser context — equivalent to a brand new browser profile. Full isolation with near-zero overhead. Save authentication state once and reuse it across tests. Resilient locators Find elements with selectors that mirror how users see the page: getByRole , getByLabel , getByPlaceholder , getByTestId . No brittle CSS paths. Parallelism and sharding Tests run in parallel by default across all configured browsers. Shard across multiple machines for faster CI. Full cross-browser coverage on every commit. Built for AI agents Accessibility snapshots, not screenshots Agents interact with pages through structured accessibility trees — element roles, names, and refs. Deterministic and unambiguous, no vision models required. MCP server Drop-in Model Context Protocol server for VS Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, and any MCP client. Full browser control through standard tool calls. CLI for coding agents Token-efficient command-line interface with installable skills. Purpose-built for Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and similar coding agents that need to balance browser automation with large codebases. Session monitoring Visual dashboard with live screencast previews of all running browser sessions. Click any session to zoom in and take control. Powerful tooling Test generator Record your actions in the browser and Playwright writes the test code. Generate assertions from the recording toolbar. Pick locators by clicking on elements. Trace Viewer Full timeline of test execution with DOM snapshots, network requests, console logs, and screenshots at every step. Investigate failures without re-running. VS Code extension Run, debug, and generate tests directly in the editor. Set breakpoints, live-inspect locators in the browser, and view full execution traces in the sidebar. Any browser. Any platform. Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Headless and headed. Also available for Python , .NET , and Java . Chosen by companies and open source projects

audit.evidenceText: Power BI Theme Generator - Create Professional Themes in Seconds | Power UI | Power UI                                        New    Custom design systems: your own tokens     Power BI themes, built like a design system  Set colours, type and spacing once as tokens. Power UI writes the theme file Power BI Desktop loads and shows it on a real Power BI report while you work: by hand, with the AI assistant, or from your coding agent.   Start Free    Watch demo     Free plan, no card   Pro and Team: pay once   Export tested against Microsoft's theme schema                             Studio     AI Assistant     Your Agent    powerui.com/studio       Data colors                Radius        8px           Revenue   $4.2M  +12.4%       Orders   18.4K  +8.1%       Margin   38.2%  +2.3%    Revenue by region                Mix       Trend             Trusted by teams at              Real reports  What a Power UI theme looks like in Power BI  Five reports built in Power BI Desktop with Power UI themes. Screenshots, not mockups; the data is sample data.    Lumon Enterprises  Orbital Solutions  Talisker Storm Logistics  Global Health & Safety Monitor  Visit the US National Parks              Lumon Enterprises   · Power BI Desktop         Open full size     On the page  Revenue by segment against last year, a share donut, a customer table with flags and a daily sales line.    The theme  The Power UI default palette, Segoe UI titles at 600, hairline borders on every card.         From customers  What people who ship reports with it say     “ Power UI enables me to quickly deliver polished, app-like reports, saving me a tremendous amount of time and effort. Now, I don't need to spend hours tweaking designs or second-guessing color choices; everything I need is right there. ”   Kimberlee Jelly  Product Manager ,  Microsoft     “ A huge thank you for Power UI! It's been critical to reducing the time it takes me to make high-quality Power BI visuals. Power UI has been key in helping me build up my consulting company. ”   Mitchell Telatnik  Founder ,  SecureMetrics.io          How it works  From design tokens to the file Power BI loads  Power UI keeps your choices as tokens and writes them into a Power BI report theme. Here is the default theme, traced through. The values are the real export.      1  Tokens      a   Data palette · Power UI                 b   @text-primary    slate 12 ·  #1C2024   Titles: Segoe UI, weight 600     c   @border-primary · @radius-default    slate 7 ·  #CDCED6  · md =  6  px    Tokens are named once and reused. Change a token once and every visual that uses it follows: the preview, the export, your whole team's reports. audit.pageTitle: Quantitative Analysis of Textual Data • quanteda
audit.pageDescription: A fast, flexible, and comprehensive framework for quantitative text analysis in R. Provides functionality for corpus management, creating and manipulating tokens and n-grams, exploring keywords in context, forming and manipulating sparse matrices of documents by features and feature co-occurrences, analyzing keywords, computing feature similarities and distances, applying content dictionaries, applying supervised and unsupervised machine learning, visually representing text and text analyses, and more.
audit.evidenceText: Quantitative Analysis of Textual Data • quanteda Skip to contents quanteda: Quantitative Analysis of Textual Data quanteda is an R package for managing and analyzing text, created and maintained by Kenneth Benoit and Kohei Watanabe . Its creation was funded by the European Research Council grant ERC-2011-StG 283794-QUANTESS and its continued development is supported by the Quanteda Initiative CIC . The package is designed for R users needing to apply natural language processing to texts, from documents to final analysis. Its capabilities match or exceed those provided in many end-user software applications, many of which are expensive and not open source. The package is therefore of great benefit to researchers, students, and other analysts with fewer financial resources. While using quanteda requires R programming knowledge, its API is designed to enable powerful, efficient analysis with a minimum of steps. By emphasizing consistent design, furthermore, quanteda lowers the barriers to learning and using NLP and quantitative text analysis even for proficient R programmers. quanteda version 4 The quanteda 4.0 is a major release that improves functionality and performance and further improves function consistency by removing previously deprecated functions. It also includes significant new tokeniser rules that makes the default tokeniser smarter than ever before, with new Unicode and ICU-compliant rules that enable it to work more consistently with even more languages. We describe more fully these significant changes in: * an article about the new external pointer tokens objects ; * an article showing performance benchmarks for the new external pointer tokens objects, as well as some of the tokeniser improvements in v4; and * the changelog for v4 a full listing of the changes, improvements, and deprecations in v4. The quanteda family of packages We completed the trend of splitting quanteda into modular packages with the release of v3. The quanteda family of packages includes the following: quanteda : contains all of the core natural language processing and textual data management functions quanteda.textmodels : contains all of the text models and supporting functions, namely the textmodel_*() functions. This was split from the main package with the v2 release quanteda.textstats : statistics for textual data, namely the textstat_*() functions, split with the v3 release quanteda.textplots : plots for textual data, namely the textplot_*() functions, split with the v3 release We are working on additional package releases, available in the meantime from our GitHub pages: quanteda.sentiment : Functions and lexicons for sentiment analysis using dictionaries quanteda.tidy : Extensions for manipulating document variables in core quanteda objects using your favourite tidyverse functions How To… Install (binaries) from CRAN The normal way from CRAN, using your R GUI or install.packages ( "quanteda" ) (New for quanteda v4.0) For Linux users: Because all installations on Linux are compiled, Linux users will first need to install the Intel oneAPI Threading Building Blocks for parallel computing for installation to work. To install TBB on Linux: # Fedora, CentOS, RHEL sudo yum install tbb - devel # Debian and Ubuntu sudo apt install libtbb - dev Windows or macOS users do not have to install TBB or any other packages to enable parallel computing when installing quanteda from CRAN. Compile from source (macOS and Windows) Because this compiles some C++ and Fortran source code, you will need to have installed the appropriate compilers to build the development version. You will also need to install TBB: macOS: First, you will need to install XCode command line tools. xcode - select -- install Then install the TBB libraries and the pkg-config utility: (after installing Homebrew ): brew install tbb pkg - config Finally, you will need to install gfortran . Windows: Install RTools , which includes the TBB libraries. Use quanteda See the quick start guide to learn how to use quanteda . Get Help Read out documentation at https://quanteda.io . Submit a question on the quanteda channel on StackOverflow . See our tutorial site . Cite the package Benoit, Kenneth, Kohei Watanabe, Haiyan Wang, Paul Nulty, Adam Obeng, Stefan Müller, and Akitaka Matsuo. (2018) “ quanteda: An R package for the quantitative analysis of textual data ”. Journal of Open Source Software . 3(30), 774. https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.00774 . For a BibTeX entry, use the output from citation(package = "quanteda") . Leave Feedback If you like quanteda , please consider leaving feedback or a testimonial here . Contribute Contributions in the form of feedback, comments, code, and bug reports are most welcome. How to contribute: Fork the source code, modify, and issue a pull request through the project GitHub page . See our Contributor Code of Conduct and the all-important quanteda Style Guide . Issues, bug reports, and wish lists: File a GitHub issue . Contact the maintainer by email. audit.pageTitle: Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes | Nieman Journalism Lab
audit.pageDescription: Allowing scraped content to be used for all "advertising and business products" is a substantial expansion of Meta's permissions.
audit.evidenceText: Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes | Nieman Journalism Lab Get Nieman Lab in your inbox. All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder. Subscribe another address Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions. Meta-owned platforms include Facebook, WhatsApp, Oculus, Threads, Instagram, and Messenger. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 17, 2026, 2:30 p.m. RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models. In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts. On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then. “I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'” Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.” Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place. As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold): You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products . Here’s the original text : You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains , web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train , and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements . The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Meta's controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 ★ Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms Adding this language to more general terms of service, and allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products,” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s scraping permissions. A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “ Ad Creative Generative AI Terms ” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand. Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements. “[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.” University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house. “You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 At least three journalism organizations have publicly raised concerns about the forthcoming terms as a result of Nieman Lab’s reporting. Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “ scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power .” The United Kingdom News Media Association , the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene. “This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber . “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.” The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “ outrageous and probably illegal .” “The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” This story has been updated to include comments from Meta. Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know: [email protected] .       Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites     
   

   
           
         Link 
         newsmediaalliance.org ↗ 
       
    
           
         Posted by 
         Hanaa' Tameez        
    
     
       October 22, 2026 
     
   
 


 
   The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30. 
 In an  open letter  to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO  Danielle Coffey  wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.” 
 The terms,  first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15 , would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta  removed  the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But  legal experts told Nieman Lab  the revised terms would still permit mass scraping. 
 “News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.” 
 NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues: 
    
 (i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content; 
 (ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products; 
 (iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized; 
 (iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected. 
   
 Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.” 
 The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent  a similar letter  to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world. 
 The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute  published  its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”

      Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook     
   

   
           
         Link 
         pewresearch.org ↗ 
       
    
           
         Posted by 
         Hanaa' Tameez        
    
     
       October 20, 2026 
     
   
 


 
   Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts. 
 According to  data  from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook. 
 That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source —  a trend  that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly  abandoning news websites for social media.  
 The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half ( 59% ) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only  19%  actually prefer social media as a place to get news. 
   
 Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%). 
 Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky. 
 The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers. 
 The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%).  The Center found that  20% of U.S. adults  now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022. 
   
 Read the full report  here .

Taking place at Tableau Conference in San Diego, three worthy contestants take center stage in front of a global audience and have 20 minutes to deliver a compelling and awe-inspiring story using the same data set. When does Iron Viz take place? Iron Viz, the world's largest data visualization competition, is held on the keynote stage at Tableau Conference every year. The three finalists are selected from a global qualifier competition, which usually happens towards the second half of the year and is open for one month. How will the winner be chosen? A panel comprised of Tableau ambassadors, previous Iron Viz finalists, data viz experts, and guest judges will evaluate all submissions based on the following criteria: Design Storytelling Analysis Analysis will be the tiebreaker in case two vizzes have the same overall score. Scores and feedback can be provided upon request by filling out this form after the contest is over. How is Iron Viz: Student Edition different from Iron Viz? Iron Viz: Student Edition is a competition open exclusively to students, though we encourage you to participate in both. audit.evidenceText: S+T+ARTS Prize Grand prize of the European Commission honoring Innovation in Technology, Industry and Society stimulated by the Arts Congratulations to the 2026 winners! All about the 2026 winners S+T+ARTS = Innovation at the Nexus of Science, Technology, and the ARTS S+T+ARTS is an initiative of the European Commission to foster alliances of technology and artistic practice that effectively implement European policymaking to nurture innovation and that benefit the art world as well. The focus is on people and projects that contribute to mastering the social, ecological and economic challenges this continent faces. One element of this S+T+ARTS Initiative is a prestigious award generously endowed with €40,000 in prize money. A yearly competition is held to single out for recognition innovative projects at the nexus of science, technology and the arts that have what it takes to make a significant impact on economic and social innovation. The two S+T+ARTS prize winners each receive €20,000 and are prominently featured at Ars Electronica and other events of the consortium partners INOVA+, French Tech Grand Provence, Media Solutions Center Baden-Württemberg, Salzburg Festival, Sonar, T6Ecosystems and Kustodie at TUD Dresden University of Technology. Winners Jury Network January 7, 2026 Submission phase for S+T+ARTS Prize 2026 begins March 9, 2026, 2 PM CET Extended Submission deadline April 16 – 19, 2026 Jury Meeting June 9, 2026 Announcement of the award winners September 9 – 13, 2026 Exhibition and talks at the Ars Electronica Festival Innovation in and for Europe Science, Technology and Arts (S+T+ARTS for short) limn a nexus at which insightful observers have identified extraordinarily high potential for innovation. And innovation is precisely what’s called for if we’re to master the social, ecological and economic challenges that Europe will be facing in the near future. In this S+T+ARTS Prize initiative, the European Commission’s focus is on projects and people that can make meaningful contributions to this effort. Art as Catalyst Here, art is assigned the role of catalyst that propagates scientific and technological knowledge and skills among the general public and triggers innovative processes. Accordingly, S+T+ARTS is emphasizing, on one hand, artistic works that influence or change the way we look at technology, and, on the other hand, very promising forms of collaboration between the private sector and the world of art and culture. A prizewinning project will be singled out for recognition in both categories and each will be supported with €20,000 prize money.

The awards have previously been scooped by reporters from the BBC, The Economist, Mail on Sunday and the Times and celebrate the great strides that have been made in journalists' use of numbers to tell a story. The awards are kindly sponsored by the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC). Read about the 2026 winners. Criteria   The awards are open to all journalists (and non-journalists for the best statistical commentary category), including those based outside the UK and are for work completed in the previous calendar year.  Categories The categories are as follows: Data visualisation  – stories which include data visualisation to aid explanation of the statistics being presented  Explaining the facts  – stories which take a current issue or statistic already published and enable greater public understanding through effective explanation  Investigative journalism  – stories which include previously unpublished statistics either through unpublished data that have been sourced and analysed by the journalist or new analyses of existing data  Best statistical commentary by a non-journalist  – this is awarded for an outstanding example of statistical analysis or explanation on a topical issue, aimed at a non-specialist audience. audit.pageTitle: Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism - The Walkley Foundation
audit.evidenceText: Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism - The Walkley Foundation Skip to main content Hit enter to search or ESC to close Close Search The Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism The Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism Entries have now closed for the 71st Walkley Awards. Finalists will be announced 15 October. Winners will be announced at the Walkley Awards in Sydney on 19 November. The Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism are presented annually in Australia to recognise and reward the best in the craft. Finalists are selected by eminent journalists and photographers and overall winners judged by the Walkley Judging Board . See all the Walkley Awards categories . The awards cover all media and have grown organically over the years, expanding to encompass the changing nature of the media industry and innovation in journalism. More than 1400 entries are received each year across 30 categories. The Walkleys also recognise excellence in longform journalism through the Walkley Book and Documentary awards. The Gold Walkley is the most prestigious award, chosen from all category winners. The Walkley Awards exist to recognise “creative and courageous acts of journalism that seek out the truth and give new insight to an issue”. They reward excellence, independence, innovation and originality in storytelling and distinctive reporting. This can be through research and investigations, well-crafted and innovative presentations, news-breaking single stories and engaging, entertaining and/or informative reporting. In 2026 all entries must have been published in Australia between 19 August, 2025 and 17 August, 2026. Eligibility for the Walkley Awards is based on independent acts of journalism, free from any commercial or corporate interests. All entries must be factually based. The Walkley Awards entry fee is $200 (except for the Walkley Book Award and Walkley Documentary Award which are $300, including GST). MEAA members still get the best deal, with free entry as part of their membership. Read the Terms & Conditions and FAQs before submitting your entry. If you have any questions please contact Margie Smithurst, margie.smithurst@walkleys.com Winners of the 70th Walkley Awards were announced on 27 November, 2025. See all the winners here . Adele Ferguson and Chris Gillett won the 2025 Gold Walkley, Australian journalism’s highest honour for a series of stories on 7.30 , Four Corners and ABC online. The Walkley Judging Board unanimously selected the pair’s multi-month multi-platform investigation into the systemic failures in childcare as the story of the year. See all the 2025 Walkley Awards finalists here . To find out when we announce finalists and winners, sign up for our weekly newsletter . The 70th Walkley Awards winners The 69th Walkley Awards winners Fine print: Walkley Awards categories Terms & Conditions FAQs Supporting Statement tips The judging process Conflict of interest guidelines Contact us Photography and longform Walkley Photography Awards The Walkley Book Award The Walkley Documentary Award Also on this page All Walkley Award Winners 1956-2024 Gold Walkley Winners Outstanding Contribution to Journalism Winners Entry Information 2026 entries open on 1 July, 2026. All entries must have been published/broadcast in Australia between 19 August, 2025 and 17 August, 2026. General criteria in assessing entries include: How the story was initiated and followed (with particular credit given for instigating or finding a story) Newsworthiness, including exclusivity Creativity and innovation Research and investigation Balance, accuracy and ethics Consideration of the resources available Consideration of production pressures, deadlines and time constraints Demonstration of best use of the format/s in which the work was published or broadcast, including clever choices in storytelling through multimedia Excellence in written or verbal communication and/or technical and production skill Public impact or benefit, including audience engagement and serving specific communities The Walkley Awards for Excellence in Photojournalism recognise visual journalists producing still photography for any platform. Criteria include storytelling, courage, public impact, creativity, innovative use of technology, technical ability and resourcefulness and can include soundslides and photofilm. Only photos taken between 19 August, 2025 and 17 August, 2026 . Each entry must contain at least one published picture. Outstanding Contribution to Journalism: Each year, the Walkley Board of Directors recognise the achievements of a person or group that has demonstrated an outstanding commitment to the highest standards of journalism – truth, rigour, integrity and fairness – over their career or period of operation. Entries open on 1 July, 2025. If you have any questions or need help please contact margie.smithurst@walkleys.com . Winners are announced at the BCS Annual Conference In association with our sponsors, we present a series of awards for excellence in cartography that are open to everyone. Entries are encouraged from those engaged in all aspects of mapping - practical, theoretical, commercial and academic - using traditional or innovative techniques and research. ​ The awards are presented at our Annual Conference. If you have any queries, contact Jim Goldsmith our Awards Officer   New Award entry forms and rules have been updated for 2026. Award and winners entries for previous years from 2016 are available in the GeoViz Resource Centre. ​ ​ The closing date for the BCS Awards has now passed and the winners will be announced at the BCS Annual Conference in Edinburgh on 9th September. Details of 2027 awards will be announced in February 2027. BCS Awards Form 2026 Peter Jolly Award Best Map / Data Visualisation Open exclusively to BCS members for any single map or geographic data visualisation in printed or digital form. This award will be judged by BCS members. The winner will be the entry that receives the most votes. Each BCS member will be allocated one vote and in the event of a tie the BCS President will have the deciding vote The closing date for this award has now passed. Peter Jolly Award Rules 2026 Peter Jolly Award Form 2026 Stanfords Award Best entry for Printed Mapping Open to any mapping in the printed form, whether it be a poster, folded sheet map, atlas, or page from a book, etc. The Stanfords Award comprises a trophy and a certificate, and is run with the support of Stanfords map and travel book store. The closing date for this award has now passed.   Stanfords Award Rules 2026 BCS Awards Form 2026 The Collins Bartholomew Award for Thematic Mapping & Infographics Best entry for Thematic Mapping & Infographics Presented for originality and excellence in the field of thematic cartography with emphasis on effective communication of the intended theme or themes. The Collins Bartholomew Award comprises a trophy, and a certificate, and is run with the support of HarperCollins. The closing date for this award has now passed. Collins Bartholomew Award Rules 2026 BCS Awards Form 2026 Ordnance Survey Student Award Qualifying entries can be from individuals doing full or part time education courses/studies. Digital Mapping Award Rules 2026 BCS Awards Form 2026 The Ian Mumford Award For university and college students This award is intended to encourage and recognise excellence in original cartographic research undertaken by university or college students who have been engaged in full or part-time study. audit.evidenceText:
Building OSINT evidence databases: Lessons from the Amnesty Digital Investigations Summit | HURIDOCS 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 
	 


 
 
 
 
		 
							 
			 
							 
		 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 
 
 
                                   
  
 
 
 
 
     
 

 
     
          

   

  
     Skip to content 

     
       
      

     

 
	 

     
			 

				    Home   >   Latest   >   News   >  Building OSINT evidence databases: Lessons from the Amnesty Digital Investigations Summit   
			 

			
 
   

           Building OSINT evidence databases: Lessons from the Amnesty Digital Investigations Summit 
    
           Reflections on organising, preserving and making open-source information usable for human rights investigations and accountability.
 
    
           
        By
                   
              Lucía Gómez           
                on  3 November 2026 
       
    
   
   
           
         
       
       
        Lucía Gómez Vicente presented a workshop on organising and storing open-source information and how to build evidence databases      

       

				 

        	
 A video disappears from social media. An account is suspended. A photograph is shared thousands of times, losing its original context along the way. For human rights investigators working with open-source information, these are everyday challenges that can determine whether information remains useful long after an event has taken place. 



 Videos, photographs, social media posts and satellite imagery can help document human rights violations, reconstruct events and support accountability efforts. Yet collecting information is only the beginning. The real challenge lies in preserving it, understanding what it can tell us and ensuring it remains accessible and reliable over time. 



   The Amnesty Digital Investigations Summit was held in Geneva from 8 to 9 October 2026.  



 At the  Amnesty Digital Investigations Summit  in Geneva on 8 and 9 October 2026, practitioners explored the methods, tools and challenges involved in open-source investigations. Drawing on HURIDOCS’ experience in human rights information management, we presented  Organising and Storing Open-Source Information: How to Build Evidence Databases , exploring how documentation methodologies, structured data and digital preservation can support investigations over the long term. 



 Four themes stood out: the importance of provenance and traceability, the need to preserve digital material early, the challenges of verification in the age of AI, and the value of designing information systems around investigators’ needs. 



  Starting with the purpose, not the technology  



 When faced with large volumes of digital information, it can be tempting to start by looking for the right tool. But an effective evidence database begins with a different question: what do we need this information to help us understand? 



 An investigation focused on criminal accountability may have different requirements from one supporting advocacy, journalism or public documentation. These differences shape how information should be collected, organised, preserved and accessed. 



 Before selecting a platform or building a data model, teams need to establish what they are documenting, how the information will be used and which relationships they need to capture between events, people, locations and sources. 



 This requires collaboration between investigators, documenters and technical teams. The goal is not to collect every possible data point, but to build a system that supports the investigation’s actual needs and can evolve as new findings emerge. 



  Connecting the dots without losing sight of the source  



 Imagine a video circulating online that appears to show an incident involving security forces. Where was it published? When was it collected? Can its location be verified? Does other material support or challenge the initial interpretation? These questions illustrate why organising evidence involves more than storing files. Investigators need to distinguish between the source itself, the information recorded about it and the claims it may support. 



 The original video is one element. Its metadata and collection history provide another. The interpretation that it depicts a particular event, location or actor is a separate conclusion requiring assessment. 



 Keeping these elements distinct allows investigators to trace conclusions back to their supporting material, connect multiple sources to an event and identify where uncertainty remains. A well-designed database makes these relationships visible without treating an investigative interpretation as an established fact. 



 This is particularly important when information may be used in accountability processes, where investigators need to explain not only what they believe happened, but how they reached their conclusions.
